title: Traffic Deaths Surge 15% on Major Album Release Days, Harvard Study Finds
excerpt: A new study published in JAMA Network Open links blockbuster album drops by Taylor Swift, Drake, and Bad Bunny to a sharp spike in fatal car crashes — with distracted smartphone use the likely culprit.
body:
• Traffic fatalities in the U.S. increased by approximately 15% on the release days of the 10 most-streamed albums between 2017 and 2022, according to a study published in JAMA Network Open.
  • Streaming activity surged more than 40% on those same days, with researchers pointing to smartphone-enabled driver distraction as the likely mechanism.
  • The effect was most pronounced among solo drivers and sober drivers — suggesting phone interaction, not alcohol or partying, was the primary factor.
  • The study was led by Indian-American physician Dr. Vishal Patel of Mass General Brigham and Harvard Medical School, who was inspired after drifting out of his lane while scrolling Spotify.

When Dr. Vishal Patel found himself scrolling through Spotify to find songs from a new Taylor Swift album while driving, he realized he had drifted out of his lane. That near-miss inspired a research question that has now produced one of the most striking findings in distracted driving research.

A new study published Monday in the journal JAMA Network Open found a 15% increase in traffic fatalities on the days major new albums are released, compared with the days immediately before and after — an increase of roughly 18 additional deaths per release day.

The Research

The study, led by Patel, a physician at Mass General Brigham and researcher at Harvard Medical School, examined the 10 albums that generated the most single-day streams on Spotify between 2017 and 2022. The list included "Midnights" by Taylor Swift, "Certified Lover Boy" by Drake, "Un Verano Sin Ti" by Bad Bunny, and works by Harry Styles, Kendrick Lamar, and Kanye West.

Researchers compared traffic fatality data from the Fatality Analysis Reporting System — a federal census of every fatal crash on U.S. public roads — against daily Spotify streaming data. They used a 10-day window before and after each album release to control for day-of-week effects, federal holidays, and other variables.

On average, there were 121 car crash fatalities on non-release dates compared with 139 deaths on album release days. Across the 10 albums studied, the pattern translated to approximately 182 excess fatal crashes linked to release days.

"Nobody had looked at album releases, which are one of the few moments when tens of millions of people reach for their phones at the same time, for the same reason, for something other than texting."

— Dr. Vishal Patel, Mass General Brigham

The Telling Pattern

What convinced researchers the finding was genuine was the pattern underneath the data. The increase in fatalities was more pronounced among drivers who were alone in the car — presumably because passengers in the front seat are more likely to handle music selection. It was also stronger among sober drivers than among those who had been drinking, and it was not concentrated at night.

"If this were really about release parties and alcohol, you'd expect the opposite on all three counts," Patel said.

The researchers also checked the same calendar dates in years when no major album was released and found no increase in fatalities, further strengthening the link between streaming surges and crashes.

Dr. Anupam Jena, a professor at Harvard Medical School and co-author of the study, acknowledged that the exact mechanism remains uncertain. "We don't know for sure what the mechanism is here. Is it that the music is louder? Is it a new album and people are just excited? Is it the mechanics of fumbling around with your phone?" he said.

Beyond Texting

The study comes as conversations about distracted driving expand well beyond texting and phone calls. More than 35,000 people die in car crashes in the U.S. each year, according to the Department of Transportation, with 3,308 fatalities attributed to distracted driving in 2022 alone.

Dr. Despina Stavrinos, director at the Institute of Social Science Research at the University of Alabama, said the study "broadens the conversation from 'Are people texting while driving?' to a much more important question: How does continuous interaction with a digital ecosystem affect driving?"

Dr. Christopher Worsham, an assistant professor at Harvard Medical School and co-author of the study, emphasized that the danger lies not in listening to music but in the physical act of interacting with a phone or infotainment system. "Queue up your music before you put the car in drive, and let it play until you can safely change it," he said.

Implications for Streaming Platforms

The researchers suggested that streaming platforms like Spotify could introduce safety features, from "nudge" notifications encouraging drivers to let passengers handle music selection to larger buttons, voice-first design, and driving-mode interfaces that minimize interaction.

Ian Reagan, a senior research scientist at the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety, noted some limitations — the study does not account for non-federal holidays like Halloween that might independently affect crash rates — but said the findings add important evidence to the growing body of research on smartphone distraction.

"These days are predictable," Patel said. "That means they're also preventable."
